summary_html: The child is **removed from the home** and placed in foster care under court order or emergency authority. Federal statutes tie funding to safety findings, judicial oversight, and permanency planning.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — removal, reasonable-efforts, and permanency requirements  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal monitoring of placement decisions

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: In re Texas Department of Family & Protective Services
key_cases.holding: The mass removal of children from the YFZ Ranch was not warranted on the evidence, because Chapter 262 requires danger to the individual child and the Family Code gives courts ample authority to protect children without separating them from their parents.
key_cases.relevance: The Texas Supreme Court's controlling application of Family Code §§ 262.101-.201 at this node: danger must be proved as to the particular child, and the court must use the Code's lesser alternatives — orders restraining a party, removing the alleged perpetrator, or assisting the investigation — before separating a family.
key_cases.quote: the Family Code gives the district court broad authority to protect children short of separating them from their parents and placing them in foster care

key_cases.case_name: M.D. ex rel. Stukenberg v. Abbott
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Texas long-term foster children have a substantive due process right to be free from an unreasonable risk of harm, and the State's caseworker-caseload and monitoring failures supported class-wide liability, although the district court's injunction was significantly overbroad.
key_cases.relevance: The controlling systemic authority for Texas: it is the Fifth Circuit's framework for caseworker caseloads, placement oversight and monitoring of children in DFPS conservatorship, and — because Suter forecloses private Title IV-E enforcement — it is the mechanism that has actually produced federal oversight of this node in Texas.
key_cases.quote: we hold that the General Class and the LFC subclass were properly certified

key_cases.case_name: Smith v. Organization of Foster Families for Equality & Reform
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: Whatever liberty interest a foster family may have is substantially attenuated when the child is being returned to the natural parents, and the State's existing pre-removal procedures satisfied due process.
key_cases.relevance: Defines how much process is due before a child is moved out of a foster home, and holds the foster family's interest is weakest when the move returns the child to the parents.
key_cases.quote: the procedures provided by New York State in § 392 and by New York City's SSC Procedure No. 5 are adequate

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The State creates a DeShaney 'special relationship' with children when it removes them from their homes and places them under its supervision, assuming a duty of constitutionally adequate care; but that relationship and any liberty interest arising from it lapse when the children are adopted, so the adoptive parents' post-adoption claims for further services failed.
key_cases.relevance: The Fifth Circuit source for the proposition that placing a child in foster care triggers an affirmative constitutional duty of care — the line Hernandez only recited. It is the case this node actually needs.
key_cases.quote: TDHS created a “special relationship” with the Griffiths’ children when it removed them from their natural homes and placed them under state supervision.

timeline_requirements.deadline: On or before the first business day after the child is taken into possession; if the court is unavailable, no later than the first business day after it becomes available and never later than the third business day — Tex. Fam. Code § 262.106(a)
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Child taken into possession in an emergency without a court order
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: The child shall be returned to the parent, managing conservator, possessory conservator, guardian, caretaker, or custodian presently entitled to possession (Tex. Fam. Code § 262.106(c))

notice_requirements.timing: Written notice to each parent of the child, or to the child's conservator or legal guardian, when a representative of the department or other agency takes possession of a child under Chapter 262: as soon as practicable, but in any event not later than the first business day after the date the child is taken into possession (Tex. Fam. Code § 262.109(a)-(b))
content_required: The reasons why the department or agency is taking possession of the child and the facts that led the department to believe the child should be taken into custody (Tex. Fam. Code § 262.109(c)(1))

The name of the person at the department or agency whom the parent, conservator, or other custodian may contact for information relating to the child or a legal proceeding relating to the child (Tex. Fam. Code § 262.109(c)(2))

A summary of the legal rights of a parent, conservator, guardian, or other custodian under Chapter 262 and an explanation of the probable legal procedures relating to the child (Tex. Fam. Code § 262.109(c)(3))
A statement that the parent, conservator, or other custodian has the right to hire an attorney (Tex. Fam. Code § 262.109(c)(4))
notice_requirements.defective_notice_consequence: Not specified in Tex. Fam. Code § 262.109. The written notice may be waived by the court at the initial hearing on a showing that the parents, conservators, or other custodians could not be located or that the department took possession of the child under Subchapter D, or for other good cause (Tex. Fam. Code § 262.109(d))
